title: Digital Literacy
heading: Digital Literacy
summary: The goal of this entry-level course is to equip students with essential digital literacy skills, important for both personal and professional success in today's digital world. By mastering basic computer and internet skills, students will improve their productivity, safety, and digital communication abilities. Even tech-savvy learners should find this course helpful.
objectives: Understand the function of basic hardware and software components.
Navigate efficiently through an operating system (Windows or macOS).
Apply best practices for digital security and privacy.
Utilize common productivity tools and cloud storage solutions.

slides: Basics of Computer Safety

Computers are complicated

It’s a miracle they even work at all! So it’s no surprise that a lot can go wrong.
Protecting your computer

Protecting yourself online

  • Don’t change passwords often - this encourages you to pick weak, easy-to-crack passwords. Instead choose a strong password the first time and use a different one for each site in case one is compromised. Keep track of your passwords (Google Chrome and iCloud Keychain).
  • Use two-factor authentication.
  • https://haveibeenpwned.com/
  • Don’t click on suspicious links. DO NOT share personal information online. (Look at some examples of phishing.)
  • Don’t open random .exe files if you don’t completely trust the source.
  • https://www.udemy.com/course/computer-literacy/learn/lecture/15741298#overview

Do I need a VPN?

Maybe (usually not.)

Nowadays it’s harder for strangers to snoop and see data; over 90% of web connections are encrypted. Very little need to waste time and money on a VPN.

If you’re not being stalked, living in a country where Internet is censored, or trying to watch Netflix shows that aren’t available in your area, you’re probably fine.

Instead use ad blockers like uBlock Origin and privacy extensions like Privacy Badger to protect yourself from advertisers.

Why is my computer slow?

  • Run Storage Sense to remove unnecessary files
  • Defragment and Optimize Drive
  • Uninstall unused programs
  • Stop programs from running on startup
  • Scan for viruses
  • Check for updates
  • Switch to “High Performance” settings
  • Check disk drive
  • If all else fails: reformat & reinstall

Backing Up Files

Backup your files regularly!!!

External Hard Drive, Windows Backup, Google Drive

units.title: Unit 2: Navigating Your OS
units.description: Become more comfortable with your operating system of choice (Windows or macOS).

slides: What is an operating system?

What does an operating system do?

Your operating system (OS) is the “system software” that manages all of the other programs on your computer.

You communicate back and forth with the OS through a user interface, and the OS in turn communicates with programs and hardware as needed.

Graphical User Interface (GUI)

Uses graphics, icons, and other visual elements to help the user interact with programs. You use a mouse to click on icons, menus, and buttons. A GUI is more visually appealing and user-friendly than a CLI, but it can also be slower and less efficient for many tasks.

Command Line Interface (CLI)

Uses text-based commands which are typed into a terminal, like old-school computers. This offers more speed and utility and flexibility compared to a GUI. This can be intimidating for people who are new to computers, so it’s recommended for advanced users for specific tasks.

Application Programming Interface (API)

An API is how programs interact with the OS, allowing them to communicate and share resources. The OS acts as a middleman or interpreter between hardware and programs, eliminating the need for programmers to write lengthy code for each program. Instead, the OS handles common tasks, and apps aren't required to know any hardware specifics.

Application Programming Interface (API)

For example, Microsoft Word doesn’t need to know how to print documents. It just sends data to the OS, which sends instructions to the printer. Programs like MS Word don’t need to take into account the thousands of different types of printers with different hardware, and printers don’t need to care about what programs are using them. This makes life easier for both users and programmers.

items.title: Slideshow - The Internet & the World Wide Web

slides:
The Internet & the World Wide Web

what’s the difference?

Internet and the World Wide Web

Internet

The Internet is a global network of interconnected computers and devices. Historically, the Internet was built on top of the existing telephone network. Today, the vast majority of Internet traffic is transmitted over fiber optic cables, which use pulses of light to transmit data over long distances.

World Wide Web

The World Wide Web (WWW) is a system of linked web pages which are accessed through the Internet. Websites are hosted on web servers, and users must enter their Uniform Resource Locator (URL) to access them. URLs are made up of a protocol, domain name, and specific page or resource.

A brief history of the Internet

The Internet wasn’t invented by a single person, but was a collaborative effort from many researchers and scientists over several decades. It was developed in the late 1960s by the US Department of Defense's Advanced Research Projects Agency (ARPA) to allow researchers to easily communicate with each other. In the ‘70s, standardized communication protocols allowed these networks to be interconnected globally, leading to the creation of the Internet.

A brief history of the Internet

The World Wide Web (WWW) was invented by Sir Tim Berners-Lee in 1989. It was designed as a way to easily share information across the Internet via hyperlinks, and was first made available to the public in 1991. In the mid ‘90s, web browsers such as Netscape Navigator and Microsoft's Internet Explorer popularized the WWW, and search engines like Yahoo! and Google revolutionized the way people found information online.

“Why do I need to know this?”

The Internet has become an integral part of our daily lives, impacting the way we communicate, access information, work, and engage with others. We can better appreciate the efforts and innovations that have shaped the digital landscape by learning about its history. We can also keep up with new technological developments, security issues, and potential future developments. Understanding the Internet and the WWW empowers us to be more informed, responsible, and adaptable digital citizens.

Bill Gates

“The Internet is becoming the town square for the global village of tomorrow.”

Slideshow - Social Networking: The Pros and Cons

slides: Social networking: the pros and cons

What is Social Media?

  • Social media is any online platform that lets users to create and share content, as well as interact with each other through comments and messages. They tend to form virtual communities based on shared interests and connections.
  • Examples include YouTube, Facebook, Instagram, Twitter, Snapchat, LinkedIn, TikTok, Pinterest, Reddit, and Discord.

What is Social Media?

  • In 2021, 70% of teenagers in the U.S. said they use social media multiple times a day, up from 34% in 2012 (Common Sense Media, 2021).
  • Social media use has been linked to both positive and negative effects on mental health, social skills, and self-esteem.
The Pros

Connectivity & Communication

  • Social media allows people to stay in touch with friends and family who live far away, and build new connections with others who share similar interests.
  • It also provide opportunities for professional networking and career development.

Access to Information

  • Social media platforms offer real-time news updates and a space for sharing ideas and opinions, allowing users to learn from different perspectives and viewpoints.
  • 48% of young adults in the U.S. get their news from social media (Common Sense Media, 2019).
  • It can also be a tool for online learning and collaboration.

Creative Expression & Self-Discovery

  • Social media provides an easy way for people to share their talents and interests with a wider audience.
  • It also allows people to to join online communities based on shared interests and values, creating a sense of belonging and connection with others who share their passions.

Business & Marketing

  • Social media platforms have become essential tools for businesses to connect with their target audience and promote their products.
  • It allows businesses to provide quick and personalized customer service, increasing customer satisfaction and improving brand reputation.
The Cons

Mental Health & Well-being

  • Social comparison and “FOMO” (fear of missing out) can be detrimental to mental health
  • 27% of teenagers feel social media negatively affects their self-esteem
  • 43% of teenagers in the U.S. report experiencing cyberbullying on social media

Mental Health & Well-being

  • Social media addiction is linked to negative mental health outcomes (self-harm, suicidal behavior, poor life satisfaction)
  • Media multitasking is linked to negative effects on cognitive control, academic performance, social skills

Source: ScienceDirect - Social media use and its impact on adolescent mental health

Privacy & Security Concerns

  • Social media platforms collect vast amounts of user data, raising privacy concerns and potential misuse of personal information.
  • Users also need to be aware of cyber threats such as phishing and identity theft, emphasizing the need for strong security measures and vigilance in online interactions.

Misinformation & Fake News

  • Social media can allow false information and fake news to spread rapidly and influence public opinion.
  • The ease of sharing content on social media platforms can contribute to the rapid dissemination of misinformation.

Misinformation & Fake News

  • Read past the headline: Check the content for more context and don’t assume that the headline provides the full picture.
  • Check the author: Verify the credibility and expertise of the source.
  • Evaluate other sources: Cross-reference the information with other reliable and reputable sources.
  • Consult experts: Reach out to those who know about the subject.
  • Check your biases: Be aware of your own biases and how they may influence your judgment of the information. Beware of echo chambers.
  • Consider if it's satire: Make sure the content isn't intended as humor or satire, as these can sometimes be mistaken for genuine news.

Decreased Productivity

  • Exposure to blue light and constant mental stimulation can disrupt the body’s production of melatonin, making it harder for the brain to wind down and prepare for sleep.
  • 45% of teenagers in the U.S. said they are online almost constantly (Pew Research Center, 2018).
Finding Balance

Finding Balance

  • Turn off notifications: Disable non-essential notifications to reduce distractions and fight the urge to constantly check your phone.
  • Set time limits: Use your device settings to allocate specific periods for social media use and avoid excessive screen time, especially before bedtime.
  • Prioritize meaningful interactions: Focus on connecting with close friends and family and minimize exposure to negative or unproductive content.
  • Cultivate offline hobbies and relationships: Participate in activities that don’t involve screens and foster face-to-face interactions to build stronger personal connections.
  • Schedule a digital detox: Regularly set aside time for unplugging from social media and electronic devices, allowing for relaxation and reconnection with offline activities.
